**European Commission opens first enforcement cases under instant payments regulation**

*The Commission has launched infringement proceedings against member states that have not transposed the Instant Payments Regulation, marking the first concrete enforcement of the October 2025 deadline.*

The European Commission's June infringements package includes proceedings against member states for failing to implement Regulation (EU) 2024/886, which requires euro-area payment service providers to offer instant credit transfers at no premium to standard transfers. The regulation's first compliance deadline passed in October 2025, and several member states have evidently not completed the necessary transposition.

Enforcement action was widely expected but its arrival matters nonetheless. It signals the Commission will not let instant payments migration drift in the way that earlier SEPA deadlines did. For payment service providers still treating the regulation's requirements as aspirational, the message is that national regulators will face pressure to act, which will flow downstream to supervised firms.

Separately, Bank of Finland data published this week shows that instant payment volumes in Finland grew materially in 2025, though from a low base, reinforcing the pattern across Europe of adoption accelerating unevenly. The Commission's willingness to pursue laggards should narrow those gaps.

*Sources: [June infringements package: key decisions](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/inf_26_1084) — European Commission | [Instant payments became more common in 2025](https://www.suomenpankki.fi/en/statistics/statistical-news/payments/2026/instant-payments-became-more-common-in-2025/) — Bank of Finland*

**Bank of America prepares real-time cross-border payments for corporate clients**

*BofA will offer instant cross-border fund transfers via Swift and its CashPro platform, extending real-time settlement beyond domestic rails for corporate, commercial and institutional clients.*

Bank of America is preparing to launch a cross-border real-time payments service for corporate, commercial and financial institution clients, using Swift connectivity and its CashPro digital banking platform. The service will allow clients to send and receive funds internationally with instant settlement.

The move reflects growing competitive pressure in transaction banking, where corporate treasurers increasingly expect real-time visibility and settlement across borders, not just domestically. Swift's own investment in instant cross-border connectivity through its platform has created the infrastructure for correspondent banks to offer these services, and BofA's adoption signals that tier-one banks now view real-time cross-border as table stakes rather than a premium differentiator.

For European corporates and their banking partners, the development underscores a broader convergence: the distinction between domestic instant payments and cross-border settlement is narrowing, and the banks that cannot offer both will lose share in cash management mandates.

*Sources: [BofA preps cross-border real-time payments service](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/47867/bofa-preps-cross-border-real-time-payments-service) — Finextra*

**PaidBy partners with Mastercard to scale cross-border account-to-account payments**

*Mastercard's open finance connectivity will underpin a new cross-border account-to-account payments partnership with PaidBy, aiming to address the fragmentation that limits merchants' ability to scale domestic pay-by-bank internationally.*

PaidBy, an account-to-account payments provider owned by Xryma Plc, has partnered with Mastercard to build cross-border account-to-account payment infrastructure. The arrangement combines Mastercard's open finance network, which connects to bank APIs across multiple markets, with PaidBy's payment orchestration and settlement layer. The announcement was made at Money20/20 Europe in Amsterdam.

The partnership targets a well-known structural problem: account-to-account payments work well domestically but become fragmented across borders, forcing merchants into separate integrations per market. Mastercard has been steadily building its open finance reach since acquiring Aiia and investing in connectivity infrastructure, and this partnership extends that strategy into cross-border merchant payments.

The broader significance is Mastercard's continued positioning as infrastructure provider for account-to-account payments, not just card rails. Each partnership of this kind reinforces the network's role as an intermediary in the account-to-account space, a deliberate hedge against the risk that pay-by-bank methods disintermediate the card schemes entirely.

*Sources: [PaidBy teams up with Mastercard to scale cross-border A2A payments](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/paidby-teams-up-with-mastercard-to-scale-cross-border-a2a-payments/) — Open Banking Expo | [PaidBy® by Xryma Plc, partners with Mastercard to scale cross-border account-to-account payments](https://www.prnewswire.com/apac/news-releases/paidby-by-xryma-plc-partners-with-mastercard-to-scale-cross-border-account-to-account-payments-302791360.html) — PR Newswire*

**CFIT launches coalition to build supported payments for vulnerable customers**

*The Centre for Finance, Innovation and Technology has formed a new industry coalition to develop a framework enabling people with learning disabilities to make payments independently with third-party safeguards.*

CFIT, the UK body funded by HM Treasury to accelerate fintech adoption, has launched a Financial Inclusion Coalition focused on developing a "supported payments" framework. The initiative aims to enable people with learning disabilities to make everyday payments themselves while allowing a trusted third party to provide oversight, guidance and safeguards. The coalition builds on CFIT's earlier work on open finance, digital company identity and SME credit access.

The project has its roots in Project Nemo, a CFIT initiative from two years ago that explored how technology could support vulnerable users in financial services. Moving from research to an industry coalition with a specific deliverable, a supported payments framework, represents a step change in ambition.

For payments firms and banks, this matters operationally. Accessibility obligations are tightening across UK financial regulation, and a standard framework for supported payments could become a de facto requirement. Firms that engage early will shape the standards rather than having to retrofit compliance later.

*Sources: [CFIT forms coalition to develop supported payments framework for learning disabled](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/47862/cfit-forms-coalition-to-develop-supported-payments-framework-for-learning-disabled) — Finextra | [CFIT launches Financial Inclusion Coalition to develop inclusive payments solutions](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/cfit-launches-financial-inclusion-coalition-to-develop-inclusive-payments-solutions/) — Open Banking Expo*

**Siemens treasury chief flags corporate open banking standards as a missing layer**

*Siemens' head of treasury technology has highlighted the absence of corporate-tailored open banking standards as a persistent barrier to API-driven treasury operations, a gap that regulation has so far not addressed.*

In an interview with Global Finance, Siemens' Heiko Nix described the integration of APIs for corporate treasury use as still hampered by the lack of open banking standards designed for corporate, rather than retail, use cases. Slight variations in bank API implementations compound the problem, creating friction that undermines the efficiency gains APIs should deliver.

The observation carries weight coming from one of Europe's largest corporates. Open banking regulation in Europe was built around retail payment accounts, and while PSD3 and the proposed Payment Services Regulation broaden the scope, corporate treasury remains largely outside the framework's direct ambitions. Treasurers at large multinationals have the resources to build bespoke connectivity; mid-market corporates do not, and the standardisation gap hits them hardest.

For banks and fintechs selling API-based treasury services, this is a competitive signal. The providers that can offer genuinely standardised, multi-bank API connectivity for corporate use cases, covering cash visibility, payment initiation and reconciliation, will capture the segment. The standards gap is a market opportunity, not just a complaint.

*Sources: [Siemens' Heiko Nix Details the Corporate Treasury Tech Upgrade](https://gfmag.com/executive-interviews/siemens-heiko-nix-corporate-treasury-tech/) — Global Finance*
